quotes.text: When we made that record with Lou five years ago, we were stunned how a seasoned artist like himself could be that impulsive. We'd do one take of something. We'd make it up as we were going along. There was this completely momentary, impulsive energy. And we'd sit there and go, 'That sounds great. I think we're on to something. Now let's start honing it.' And he'd go, 'Fuck it! We're done. I'm happy. That was great. It was a moment.' And so I think that that kind of acceptance of just the moment was something that we had never experienced that close up. And I think that it definitely just gave us a new way to interpret a creative process, or gave us an additional layer, that one can be that impulsive and one can also be happy that what happened in that minute. It has a beautiful element to it that's just part of that minute. It can be different, but can it be better? But being with Lou and the way that he would just sing one take, or whatever, and then just go, 'Great. I'm happy.' It was so cool.
Having the honour of Lou Reed in our studio, steering the ship and how he worked. He was a true artist.
That moment happened, we recorded it, he wasn't doing it again – 'I don't think I could do it again, and if I could it's just going to be confusing. I've done it.'
You can get very analytical, pathologise everything that happens all the time. but that's what makes art art.
If you're the creator, then when you say you're done, you're done.
I don't like the word 'jamming' – but creating together and seeing what happens? There was not a lot of that in Metallica until Lulu showed up.
Lou was a writer at heart, and during this period he considered giving up music to follow this path.
His introductions to the pieces also gave us great insight into his creative process.
